title: Why This American Highway Dives Under the Sea
sources: Crater outline: approximate, after USGS and the Earth Impact Database

paragraphs.text: You leave the shore of Virginia Beach and the road runs straight out to sea. Low concrete, a few feet of railing, and water on both sides. After a few miles the land behind you is a thin line. Ahead, the highway runs onto a tiny island, about five acres of rock and sand in the middle of the bay. And then the road tips down and disappears into the water.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel, Virginia Beach Area.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Virginia Beach and the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (14).jpg
File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (12).jpg

shots.on_screen_text: Two islands at Thimble Shoal Channel
An island of rock and sand

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (7).jpg

paragraphs.text: This is the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel. Seventeen point six miles from shore to shore, across the mouth of the largest estuary in the United States. Twice on the way across, it dives under the sea, and while you drive through the tunnel, a cargo ship or a navy destroyer can pass over your head.

shots.on_screen_text: The Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel from orbit

stat.label: Shore to shore across the mouth of the bay

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (5).jpg

File:US Navy 031109-N-6278K-002 The USS George Washington (CVN 73), sails past the Chesapeake Bay Bridge Tunnel on the way to sea, as it prepares for the Composite Training Unit Exercise (COMPTUEX) in the Atlantic Ocean.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: USS George Washington passing the crossing, 2003 (U.S. Navy)

paragraphs.text: Most people ask how they built it. The better question is why it had to be built like this at all. Why is there seventeen miles of open water here, with two deep channels cut through it? Why would anyone pay to send a highway under the sea, when a bridge would have been cheaper? The answers go back to a rock from space, an ice age, and the largest naval base in the world. And there is one more thing, which we will come to at the end. There is a tide gauge on this crossing. Since nineteen seventy-five, the sea it measures has risen by about a foot.

shots.photo: File:Tight and Light - Kite Over The Chesapeake Bay Bridge Tunnel.jpg
File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (13).jpg

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (8).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Where the road leaves the surface
Under the mouth of the bay

chapters.title: A Hole Older Than the Bay

paragraphs.text: About thirty-five million years ago, there was no Chesapeake Bay. The coast of North America ran much farther inland, roughly where Richmond is today, and everything east of it was shallow sea. Then, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, an asteroid or comet a few miles wide came down into that sea, right about where the mouth of the bay is now.

stat.label: Since an asteroid or comet hit the lower bay

paragraphs.text: The impact blasted a crater that is among the twenty largest known on Earth. Glassy drops of melted rock rained down as far away as Texas and the Caribbean. Tsunamis spread across most of the North Atlantic. And then, over millions of years, the hole slowly filled in. Today the crater lies buried under a thousand to fifteen hundred feet of sand, mud and rock. You cannot see it from the road. But it never really went away.

shots.photo: File:Boundaries of the Chesapeake Bay impact crater.png
shots.on_screen_text: The buried Chesapeake Bay impact crater

stat.label: Among the largest known impact structures on Earth

shots.photo: File:Bediasite (35 Ma, Late Eocene; southeastern Texas) 3.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Bediasite: impact glass found in Texas

stat.label: Of sediment and rock now cover the crater

shots.on_screen_text: Above the crater today: Cape Charles

shots.photo: File:1853 U.S.C.S. Map of Cape Charles and Vicinity, Virginia - Geographicus - CapeCharles-uscs-1853.jpg

paragraphs.text: Its rim is still there under the ground, and the rubble inside it kept settling for millions of years, so the land above it stayed a little lower than the land around it. The National Park Service puts it simply: this large depression helped determine where the Chesapeake Bay would form, millions of years later. The rock from space did not dig the bay. It left a low spot, and the rivers found it.

stat.label: "Helped determine the location of the Chesapeake Bay"

shots.on_screen_text: The James and the York bend toward the bay

paragraphs.text: The bay itself is young. About twenty thousand years ago, at the height of the last ice age, so much water was locked up in ice sheets that the sea stood far below where it is now. The shore lay far to the east, out on what is now the seafloor. Where the bay is now, there was a river valley. The Susquehanna River ran down it, joined by the Potomac, the Rappahannock, the York and the James, and flowed out across dry land to a distant shore.

shots.photo: File:Old Cape Henry Lighthouse (27866899213).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Cape Henry, the south cape of the bay

stat.label: Height of the last ice age

shots.on_screen_text: Today's shore; the ice-age coast lay far offshore

shots.photo: File:A Ferry Scene on the Susquehanna at Wright's Ferry, near Havre de Grace MET DT1813.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The Susquehanna near Havre de Grace (19th-century painting)
Where the old river left the land

paragraphs.text: Then the ice melted, and the ocean came back. By about ten thousand years ago, the rising sea had flooded the lower end of that valley. The water kept climbing up the old river and its branches, until about three thousand years ago the bay reached roughly the shape it has today. A drowned river system, opening to the Atlantic through one wide gap.

shots.photo: File:New Cape Henry Lighthouse (28482794045).jpg

stat.label: The sea floods the lower river valley
The bay reaches roughly its present shape

shots.photo: File:Chesapeakelandsat.jpeg
shots.on_screen_text: The Chesapeake Bay, the largest estuary in the U.S.

paragraphs.text: That gap is where the bridge-tunnel crosses. And the drowned river did not disappear. The Geological Survey notes that remnants of the old Susquehanna still run along the bottom of the bay as a deep channel. Big ships need deep water. That is the first part of the answer. The road had to cross a seventeen-mile mouth, and it had to cross the deep paths that ships still follow. Which raises the next question: who needed to cross it so badly?

shots.on_screen_text: The gap at the mouth of the bay

shots.photo: File:US Navy 040120-N-6278K-001 USS George Washington (CVN 73) sails past the Chesapeake Bay Bridge tunnel into the Atlantic Ocean to start her deployment.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: USS George Washington heading for sea, 2004 (U.S. Navy)

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (16).jpg

paragraphs.text: Look at the map again. North of the bay's mouth is a long, flat peninsula, shared by Delaware, Maryland and Virginia. Its southern tip is the Eastern Shore of Virginia, two counties of farms, fishing villages and marsh. To reach the rest of Virginia, the people who lived there had a choice. Drive north and all the way around the bay, a trip of hours. Or take a boat.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (1).jpg
File:The S. S. Princess Anne Ferry Boat between Kiptopeke Beach and Norfolk, Virginia (8618851013).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Princess Anne, one of the bay ferries (postcard)

paragraphs.text: For most of the twentieth century, the boat was a ferry. By the late years of the service, the crossing ran from Little Creek near Norfolk to Kiptopeke, near Cape Charles. A ferry could carry about sixty cars and took about ninety minutes for the eighteen-mile trip. In fog or a hard wind, the boats waited, and so did everyone on them.

shots.on_screen_text: The ferry route across the mouth
Little Creek, the southern ferry landing

stat.label: For the 18-mile ferry crossing
stat.note: Up to about 60 cars a trip

shots.photo: File:Aerial of concrete ships in Bay (12680358583).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Old concrete ships sunk as a breakwater at Kiptopeke

paragraphs.text: In nineteen fifty-four, Virginia created a public commission to take over the ferries, and soon it was asked a bigger question. Could the mouth of the bay be crossed by road? A few miles to the west, the answer was already being built. In nineteen fifty-seven, the Hampton Roads Bridge-Tunnel opened, a three and a half mile crossing that ran out on trestles and then dived under the channel into Norfolk harbor. It proved a road could go under a shipping lane. The Chesapeake crossing would have to do it twice, on a crossing five times as long.

stat.label: Virginia creates a commission to take over the ferries

shots.photo: File:Aerial (12680379975).jpg
File:USS Dwight D. Eisenhower departs Norfolk, crossing over the - Hampton Roads Bridge Tunnel 130221-N-GC639-125.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A carrier passing over the Hampton Roads tunnel, 2013 (U.S. Navy)

paragraphs.text: But why not simply build a very tall bridge? Engineers built tall bridges all over the country in the nineteen fifties. Here, though, someone else had a say. And they were the most powerful neighbor on the bay.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (10).jpg
File:Aerial view of the Chesapeake Bay Bridge, connecting Annapolis with Maryland's Eastern Shore LCCN2011635445.tif

paragraphs.text: Just inside the mouth of the bay is Hampton Roads, one of the great natural harbors of the world, where the James and the Elizabeth rivers meet the bay. And on its southern shore, on the grounds of a nineteen-oh-seven world's fair, the United States Navy built a base in nineteen seventeen. It grew into Naval Station Norfolk, which the Navy describes as the world's largest naval installation, home port of aircraft carriers, destroyers and dozens of other ships.

shots.on_screen_text: The piers of the naval base

shots.photo: File:US Navy 110707-N-XZ912-104 An aerial view of Norfolk Naval Station, the largest naval base in the world.jpg
File:9 Flattops at Norfolk naval base, December 20, 2012.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Nine carriers at Norfolk, December 2012 (U.S. Navy)

paragraphs.text: The big ships reach the Atlantic through one deep, dredged path, the Thimble Shoal Channel, straight across the line where the crossing would have to go. In the middle of the Cold War, that made a bridge a problem. According to histories of the project, the Navy objected to any bridge over the channel. If a bridge collapsed, by accident, in a storm or through sabotage, the wreckage could close the channel and trap the fleet inside the bay.

shots.on_screen_text: From the base to the open sea

shots.photo: File:US Navy Amphibious Group underway in April 1964.jpg

File:US Navy 031109-N-6278K-002 The USS George Washington (CVN 73), sails past the Chesapeake Bay Bridge Tunnel on the way to sea, as it prepares for the Composite Training Unit Exercise (COMPTUEX) in the Atlantic Ocean.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: The channel the Navy needed open
One channel between the fleet and the Atlantic

paragraphs.text: There was a second channel too, farther north, the Chesapeake Channel, which carried ships up the bay to Baltimore. Maryland officials wanted that one kept clear as well. So the plan became a chain. Long, low trestles across the shallow water. Two higher bridges over smaller channels. And at the two places where the big ships pass, the road would leave the surface and go under them.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (11).jpg
File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (17).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A high bridge over a smaller channel

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (5).jpg

paragraphs.text: But a tunnel needs a place to start. There is no land at the edge of a shipping channel in the middle of a bay, only open water. So before anyone could build a tunnel, they had to build the ground it would start from. Four islands, in the open sea.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (6).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: An island at the mouth of a tunnel

shots.photo: File:Virginia Brunnel04.jpg

paragraphs.text: First, the money. In nineteen sixty, the commission sold two hundred million dollars in bonds to private investors, to be paid back by the tolls drivers would pay. According to the crossing's own history, no local, state or federal tax money went into the construction. If the road failed to earn its tolls, the investors would lose, not the taxpayers.

stat.label: In revenue bonds sold to private investors, 1960

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (2).jpg

stat.label: Local, state or federal tax money in the construction

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (3).jpg

paragraphs.text: Work began in the autumn of nineteen sixty. To make each island, crews first built rings of rock on the bottom of the bay, then pumped sand into the middle until it rose above the water. Then they covered the outside with armor. Granite boulders of two to four tons each, brought from a quarry in central Virginia. Each island ended up about five and a quarter acres, roughly the size of four football fields.

stat.label: Construction begins

shots.photo: File:Virginia Brunnel02.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Granite armour and a plaque on an island

stat.label: Each of the four islands

paragraphs.text: The tunnels were not dug. They were built somewhere else and sunk into place. Steel tubes, each about three hundred feet long and thirty-five feet across, were made at a shipyard in Orange, Texas, sealed at the ends so they would float, and towed all the way around Florida to Virginia. Thirty-seven of them for each tunnel. On the way, two broke away from their tugs in the Gulf of Mexico, and both were caught again.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (8).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: A tunnel under a shipping channel

stat.label: Each steel tube section; 35 feet across
Steel tube sections for each tunnel

paragraphs.text: At Norfolk the tubes got a thick shell of concrete. Then, one by one, they were sunk into a trench dug across the bottom of each channel, joined underwater, pumped dry, and buried. When it was done, ships could pass over the tunnels with no idea that a highway lay underneath.

shots.on_screen_text: The tubes lie under the channel

shots.photo: File:US Navy 040120-N-6278K-001 USS George Washington (CVN 73) sails past the Chesapeake Bay Bridge tunnel into the Atlantic Ocean to start her deployment.jpg

paragraphs.text: The trestles were a different problem. There is no bedrock to stand on here. Under the bay is the fill of that old crater and the sediments that came after it, and solid rock lies more than six thousand feet down. So the concrete piles hold the road up by friction alone, gripping the mud. The longest was driven a hundred and seventy-two feet deep.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (9).jpg

shots.on_screen_text: The bay mouth lies over the crater

stat.label: Down to bedrock under the bay mouth

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (4).jpg

stat.label: The deepest pile

paragraphs.text: Then, in March of nineteen sixty-two, the Atlantic tested the project. A nor'easter stalled off the coast for days, the storm later called the Ash Wednesday Storm. Tides ran high through Norfolk, waves broke over the work sites, and according to reporting from the time, the storm stripped away great amounts of fill and sand, knocked over a tunnel section, and wrecked the crew's main pile driver, a giant platform called the Big D.

stat.label: The Ash Wednesday Storm

shots.on_screen_text: The work sites at the mouth of the bay

shots.photo: File:Virginia Brunnel05.jpg
File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (13).jpg

paragraphs.text: The work went on. On April fifteenth, nineteen sixty-four, forty-two months after construction began, the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel opened. The ferries were retired. The next year, a competition among more than a hundred major projects named it one of the Seven Engineering Wonders of the Modern World. Accounts of the project say seven workers died building it.

stat.label: The bridge-tunnel opens, 42 months after work began

shots.photo: File:Fisherman Island National Wildlife Refuge, VA. Credit- USFWS (11804450384).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Fisherman Island, at the crossing's north end (USFWS)

stat.label: Named one of the Seven Engineering Wonders of the Modern World

shots.on_screen_text: The north end of the crossing

shots.photo: File:Virginia Brunnel01.jpg

paragraphs.text: For the first time, the Eastern Shore was joined to the rest of Virginia by road. But the bay had not agreed to anything. And it was about to make that clear.

shots.on_screen_text: Fisherman Island, the Eastern Shore end

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (15).jpg

paragraphs.text: The trestles stand in open water, and the ships that wait to enter Hampton Roads anchor all around them. In the night of January twenty-first, nineteen seventy, a gale came up. According to a later account from the Hampton Roads Naval Museum, gusts reached thirty-five to fifty knots, and six other ships dragged their anchors that night. One of them was the Navy cargo ship Yancey.

stat.label: A gale over the mouth of the bay

shots.photo: File:US Navy Amphibious Group underway in April 1964.jpg
File:USS Yancey (AKA-93) underway c1952.jpg

paragraphs.text: The Yancey's anchor would not hold. The wind pushed her across the bay, stern first, and at one thirty-seven in the morning she hit the trestle. At three thirty she hit it again, and went through. She left a gap of about four hundred feet in the road. The crossing had stockpiled spare seventy-five-foot spans, and that helped, but in the cold and the heavy seas it was still about six weeks before the road reopened. It was not the first ship to strike the trestle, and it would not be the last.

stat.label: First impact; at 3:30 she went through
Of trestle knocked out

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (12).jpg
File:Fisherman Island National Wildlife Refuge, VA. Credit- USFWS (11804792806).jpg

paragraphs.text: Then there is the wind itself. The crossing runs across open water, and nothing breaks the wind coming off the Atlantic. So it has rules you will find on very few roads. At thirty-five miles an hour of wind, the speed limit drops to forty-five and passing is banned. At forty, motorcycles, campers, anything being towed, box trucks, buses and empty tractor-trailers are turned away. At fifty, only cars, empty pickups, minivans and SUVs may cross. At sixty, the crossing closes.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio.jpg

stat.label: Speed limit 45, no passing
Motorcycles, campers, towed loads, box trucks, buses, empty trucks banned
Only cars, empty pickups, minivans and SUVs

paragraphs.text: Even so, vehicles have gone over the side more than a dozen times since the nineteen eighties, most of them trucks. By one count, at least twenty people have died in them. Some crashes came in high wind. Others came on calm days, when a driver swerved, a tire blew, or a truck simply drifted.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (11).jpg

stat.label: People killed in over-the-side crashes, by one count to 2023

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (10).jpg

paragraphs.text: For thirty-five years, the whole crossing was one two-lane road, one lane each way, with nothing in between. In nineteen ninety-nine, a second, parallel trestle opened, and each direction got its own bridge. But not its own tunnel. The new tunnels were left out to save money. So even today, when you reach an island, four lanes squeeze into two, and you drive under the sea in a single tube, with traffic coming toward you a few feet away.

stat.label: One two-lane road, one lane each way

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (17).jpg
File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (7).jpg
File:Virginia Brunnel06.jpg

paragraphs.text: The fix is a second tunnel. In twenty sixteen, the crossing signed a contract worth about seven hundred and fifty-seven million dollars for a new tube under Thimble Shoal Channel. This time it would not be sunk into a trench across a channel used by the Navy. It would be bored underneath it, by a German-built tunnel boring machine forty-three feet across and three hundred and eight feet long. Its name, chosen by a schoolgirl in a public contest, was Chessie.

shots.on_screen_text: Thimble Shoal: the new tunnel runs beside the old one

stat.label: Contract for a second tunnel under Thimble Shoal Channel, 2016

shots.photo: File:USS Dwight D. Eisenhower departs Norfolk, crossing over the - Hampton Roads Bridge Tunnel 130221-N-GC639-125.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Navy ships use the channels above

stat.label: Across the cutterhead; the machine is 308 ft long

shots.on_screen_text: Island 1, where the new tunnel begins

paragraphs.text: Chessie started mining in February twenty twenty-three. In May, it hit something it could not cut. It turned out to be a large ship's anchor, buried in the mud of the channel, made in England around the turn of the twentieth century. Some ship lost it there, long ago, at the mouth of a busy harbor.

stat.label: Chessie starts mining
A ship's anchor made in England, buried in the channel

shots.on_screen_text: The mouth of a busy harbor

shots.photo: File:New Cape Henry Lighthouse (28482794045).jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Cape Henry, at the harbor mouth

paragraphs.text: Removing it, deep under the channel, safely, took eight more months of work. Tunnelling only resumed in May twenty twenty-four, at about fifty feet a day. On January twenty-seventh, twenty twenty-five, after more than six thousand three hundred feet, Chessie broke through into its receiving pit on the second island. The crossing's current forecast for opening the new tunnel is early twenty twenty-eight.

stat.label: Of extra work to remove the anchor
From May 2024
Mined before breakthrough, 27 January 2025
Forecast opening of the new tunnel

paragraphs.text: And that is only one of the two tunnels. The second, under the Chesapeake Channel, is still decades away. So the bay keeps doing what it has done for millions of years. It slows things down. Which brings us back to the number from the beginning.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (16).jpg

paragraphs.text: Across the water from the first island is a tide gauge at Sewells Point, on the Navy base in Norfolk. It has measured the sea there since nineteen twenty-seven, almost a hundred years. Over that time, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the average sea level has risen at about one point nine inches every ten years. That adds up to about a foot and a half since the gauge went in.

stat.label: The Sewells Point tide gauge starts recording
Per decade, Sewells Point, 1927-2025
Since 1927 (1.90 in per decade x 9.8 decades)

paragraphs.text: We compared that with every tide gauge NOAA lists on the Atlantic coast of the United States whose record goes back to the nineteen thirties or earlier. There are twenty-three. Sewells Point has the fastest rise of all of them. Faster than New York, faster than Boston, almost twice as fast as Key West. And the gauge on the bridge-tunnel itself, out in the channel, has measured about two point four inches per decade since nineteen seventy-five. About a foot in fifty years.

chart.title: Sea level trend, long-record U.S. Atlantic gauges
chart.source: Own ranking of NOAA tide gauge trends

stat.label: Per decade at the bridge-tunnel gauge, 1975-2025

paragraphs.text: Part of that is the ocean rising everywhere. But here the land is also going down. The U.S. Geological Survey says coastal Virginia has the highest rates of relative sea level rise on the entire Atlantic coast, because the ground is sinking at the same time. Much of it comes from pumping. For decades, towns and industry have drawn water from deep aquifers, and as the water comes out, the clay layers squeeze together and the land settles. Part of it is the slow sag of the crust as it adjusts to the vanished ice sheets of the north. And researchers studying the sinking around Hampton Roads list one more cause among the others: ongoing shifts in the buried crater.

shots.photo: File:Chesapeake Bay Bridge–Tunnel connects Virginia Beach Hampton Roads to the Delmarva Peninsula - panoramio (15).jpg

stat.label: Relative sea level rise on the Atlantic coast: coastal Virginia
stat.source: USGS, land subsidence in coastal Virginia

shots.photo: File:Tangier Island flooding.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Tangier Island, Virginia: high water in the streets, 2023
Suffolk and Franklin: wells and sinking ground

stat.label: Measured sinking, Franklin and Suffolk, 1979-1995

paragraphs.text: The crater is still there in other ways too. Deep under the bay, the rock is soaked in water that is about twice as salty as today's ocean. In twenty thirteen, USGS scientists showed that it is seawater from the Early Cretaceous, the time of the dinosaurs, a hundred to a hundred and forty-five million years old, trapped and kept in place partly by the shattered rock of the impact.

shots.photo: File:Boundaries of the Chesapeake Bay impact crater.png

stat.label: As salty as today's ocean: water deep in the crater
Age of the seawater trapped in the crater

shots.photo: File:1853 U.S.C.S. Map of Cape Charles and Vicinity, Virginia - Geographicus - CapeCharles-uscs-1853.jpg
shots.on_screen_text: Cape Charles, above the crater (1853 chart)

paragraphs.text: So this is why the highway dives under the sea. A rock from space left a low spot. An ice age carved a river valley through it, and the melting ice drowned it. The deepest parts of the drowned river became shipping channels. And a navy that needed those channels open made the road go underneath.

shots.photo: File:US Navy 110707-N-XZ912-104 An aerial view of Norfolk Naval Station, the largest naval base in the world.jpg

paragraphs.text: The islands were built in the early nineteen sixties for the sea of the early nineteen sixties. Since then the water around them has risen by about a foot, and the ground under Norfolk is still sinking. The next tunnel under the Chesapeake Channel is planned for decades from now. So here is the question to leave in the comments: should it be built for the sea we have today, or for the sea of twenty one hundred?

shots.photo: File:Island 1 and Western Section of Bridge - panoramio.jpg
File:Tight and Light - Kite Over The Chesapeake Bay Bridge Tunnel.jpg

ask.text: Should the next tunnel be built for today's sea, or the sea of 2100?

youtube.title: Why This American Highway Dives Under the Sea
youtube.description: At the mouth of the Chesapeake Bay, a highway runs 17.6 miles out to sea, onto islands built in open water, and twice dives under the shipping channels. Why build it like that? We follow the answer from orbit: an asteroid crater buried under the bay 35 million years ago, the drowned valley of the Susquehanna, the ferries of the Eastern Shore, the Navy's fear of a fallen bridge, four man-made islands and steel tubes towed from Texas, the 1962 storm, the night USS Yancey went through the trestle, the tunnel machine Chessie and the century-old anchor it hit, and the tide gauges that show the sea rising faster here than anywhere else on the U.S. Atlantic coast.
youtube.pinned_comment: Should the next tunnel be built for today's sea, or the sea of 2100?
